headline: Nyatt Point to Conimicut: bunker stacks the bay, bass and blues follow it in
subhead: The bunker schools we said would tighten up under the new moon are here — now the question is how long the bay can hold them.
body_markdown:
Down at the piers this week the talk was all bunker. Guys hauling cast nets off the Providence River bulkheads were coming up with pods so thick the water looked like it was boiling from underneath, and that's the tell every bay rat waits for come mid-September. We flagged this last week — said the bunker schools tightening in the lower bay under the building moon were setting up the season's first real fall blitz, and that's exactly what's playing out from Nyatt Point down through Conimicut.

The tide's the engine behind all of it right now. We're a few days off the new moon and the range is still building, which means more water moving harder through the upper bay on every swing. That pulls bunker off the flats and funnels them along current lines where stripers and blues don't have to work for a meal — they just sit on the seam and let the tide do the sorting. Water's holding in that comfortable upper-60s range, not too warm to slow the bite, not cold enough yet to shut off the fluke, so for the next stretch you've got two migrations overlapping — early fall bass and blues stacking on bait, and the last gasp of summer fluke still working the sand before they slide out toward the channel.

Striped bass have been the most consistent story. Rocky Point and the flats off Conimicut have both been holding bunker pods on the last two hours of the ebb, and that's when the bigger fish show up underneath them. Snag-and-drop with a treble on 20-pound mono is still the go-to for getting a live bunker down to the fish holding under the school, but guys working bunker spoons — the 3-ounce silver ones — off the drift at Nyatt Point have been just as effective without the hassle of keeping bait alive. Fish have run mostly mid-20s to low-30-inch class, with a few better ones mixed in on the deeper edges toward the Providence River shipping channel where the bottom drops to 25-30 feet. Nothing epic yet, but steady enough that it's worth the trip if you can fish that last push of the outgoing.

Bluefish are the ones putting on the show. The same bunker schools pulling bass into the bay are getting hammered from above by blues that showed up heavier than usual for this point in September — the kind of fish chopping bait into pieces on the surface rather than picking at it. Rocky Point and the mouth of Greenwich Bay have both seen surface blitzes in the last week, mostly on the last of the flood into the top of the tide. Bucktails and poppers thrown into the chaos are getting hit fast; don't overthink the color, they're not being picky right now.

Fluke are still around, but the window's closing and the bite has gone patchy rather than steady. Prudence Island's western flats and the sandy stretches inside Greenwich Bay are still giving up keepers on the outgoing, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along the bottom in 15 to 20 feet. A few guys working live killies off Conimicut have done better than the artificial crowd, which tells you the fish are getting choosier as the water starts its seasonal slide. If fluke are the target, this is the week to go — another cold night or two and that bite starts thinning out fast as the bay pushes them toward the East Passage and out past Beavertail.

Scup have been the dependable bycatch on every trip, and honestly the most consistent producer of the week if you're just looking to fill a cooler. The rocky ledges off Nyatt Point and the structure ringing Prudence Island are holding good numbers on squid strips and clam bellies, fished light on 10-pound braid with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current. These fish don't care about the moon phase the way the bass do — they're just sitting on structure eating, and that's been true all summer.

Weakfish have shown up here and there as an incidental catch working the same bunker schools, mostly smaller fish taken on soft plastics meant for bass, nothing worth planning a trip around yet but worth knowing they're mixed in.

Looking at the next few days, the tidal range keeps building toward the full swing of this moon cycle, and that should tighten the bunker schools even further and push the blitz activity from sporadic to more predictable — probably showing up reliably on the last two hours of ebb at Rocky Point and Conimicut. If the wind stays out of the north and holds the water clean, that's the window to be there. If it swings onshore and stirs up the upper bay, shift toward Greenwich Bay and Prudence Island where the water clears faster. Either way, the fall run is building the way it's supposed to this time of year — the bait's here, the tide's cooperating, and the fish are following the script.
